brief.topic: An Infinite Sum with Only Two Loose Ends

s01: Here is a sum that keeps growing: one half, one sixth, one twelfth, one twentieth.
The denominators come from neighboring whole numbers multiplied together.
How can we understand the whole sum without adding every fraction?
Try writing one sixth as one half minus one third.
Use a common denominator: three sixths minus two sixths.
The same idea works for any neighboring pair.
One divided by n, minus one divided by the quantity n plus one, leaves one divided by their product.
Write the first four terms this way.
The negative half meets the next positive half.
The thirds cancel too, and then the quarters.
Only the first one and the final negative fifth remain.
The sum is four fifths.
Add another term: one fifth minus one sixth.
The old loose end cancels, and a new one takes its place.
After N terms, the sum is one minus one divided by the quantity N plus one.
That is an exact statement about a finite sum.
As N grows, the remaining gap approaches zero.
The infinite sum therefore converges to one.
This is called telescoping.
We first simplify each finite sum, then take its limit.
A long calculation can become manageable when we see what disappears.

scenes.narration:
Here is a sum that keeps growing: one half, one sixth, one twelfth, one twentieth. The denominators come from neighboring whole numbers multiplied together. How can we understand the whole sum without adding every fraction?

Try writing one sixth as one half minus one third. Use a common denominator: three sixths minus two sixths. The same idea works for any neighboring pair. One divided by n, minus one divided by the quantity n plus one, leaves one divided by their product.

Write the first four terms this way. The negative half meets the next positive half. The thirds cancel too, and then the quarters. Only the first one and the final negative fifth remain. The sum is four fifths.

Add another term: one fifth minus one sixth. The old loose end cancels, and a new one takes its place. After N terms, the sum is one minus one divided by the quantity N plus one. That is an exact statement about a finite sum.

As N grows, the remaining gap approaches zero. The infinite sum therefore converges to one. This is called telescoping. We first simplify each finite sum, then take its limit. A long calculation can become manageable when we see what disappears.
